introduction_markdown: Time allowed: two and a half hours. Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour and Section II in 1 1/2 hours; you are advised to divide your time accordingly. In Section II answer EITHER the a, b and c OR the d, e and f of each question. For your guidance the approximate mark(s) for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Where necessary, assume: the acceleration of free fall, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; the speed of light in air, $c = 3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the charge on an electron, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. Non-programmable calculators are allowed.

questions.enonce_markdown: Distinguish between a conductor and a semiconductor. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **conductor** (for example copper) has a very large number of free electrons at all temperatures, so it has a very low resistance (high conductivity), and its conductivity *decreases* when its temperature rises.

A **semiconductor** (for example silicon or germanium) has very few free charge carriers at room temperature, so its conductivity lies between that of a conductor and that of an insulator, and its conductivity *increases* when its temperature rises or when it is doped.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Compare n-type and p-type semiconductors in terms of:

- doping material used at production, and
- majority charge carriers. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
| | n-type semiconductor | p-type semiconductor |
|---|---|---|
| Doping material | A **pentavalent** (group V) impurity with 5 valence electrons, such as phosphorus, arsenic or antimony (a donor) | A **trivalent** (group III) impurity with 3 valence electrons, such as boron, aluminium or gallium (an acceptor) |
| Majority charge carriers | **Free electrons** (negative) | **Holes** (positive) |

In an n-type material each impurity atom gives one extra electron that is free to move, so electrons are in the majority. In a p-type material each impurity atom leaves a missing electron (a hole) in the bonds, so holes are in the majority.

questions.enonce_markdown: State how the conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor can be increased. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown: By **doping** it, that is, adding a small amount of a suitable impurity (a pentavalent or trivalent element). Raising its temperature (or illuminating it) also increases its conductivity because more charge carriers are freed.
